home.title: Make the next business move with a clearer plan.
home.summary: Start with the operating constraint or outcome. Compare practical paths, readiness questions, and the right next resource without guessing at approvals or outcomes.

families.title: Buy or sell a business
families.summary: Move a business transaction forward with a clearer view of value, readiness, diligence, structure, and capital questions.
families.problem: A transaction combines financial, operational, legal, and timing questions. Missing one can change the diligence plan or terms.
families.goal: Build an evidence-based transaction plan before making or accepting a commitment.
signals: Value expectations are not tied to consistent financial records.
The buyer or seller has not set a diligence scope.
Financing, working capital, or transition needs are still assumptions.
questions: What must be verified before a letter of intent or price discussion?
Which records and operating dependencies could change the decision?
Who should independently review legal, tax, and financing terms?
paths: Separate valuation assumptions from verified earnings and assets.
Set a diligence workplan with owners, source records, and decision gates.
Use qualified legal, tax, and financing professionals for transaction-specific advice.
children: Clarify the buyer's goals, operating capacity, target criteria, and diligence plan before pursuing a transaction.
Prepare a seller's records, transition plan, and decision criteria before entering buyer discussions.
Frame a valuation discussion around normalized earnings, assets, market evidence, and assumptions that need verification.
Check whether the buyer's goals, capital plan, operator capacity, and diligence process are ready for a search.
Organize financial records, operating dependencies, ownership decisions, and transition considerations ahead of a sale.
Stress-test a proposed transaction using verified cash flow, purchase terms, transition costs, and downside cases.
Plan a documented review of financial, legal, tax, customer, employee, and operating exposures.
Compare how cash at close, seller financing, contingencies, and transition terms shift risk between parties.
Map the transaction's sources, uses, timing, and documentation questions before discussing financing routes.
Identify owner goals, business dependencies, value drivers, and transition work that can affect exit options.

families.title: Automate funding operations
families.summary: Find the handoff slowing your funding operation, then design a small, reviewable improvement before connecting systems.
families.problem: Funding work often crosses intake, review, documents, routing, and follow-up without a single visible owner for each handoff. Re-entry and unclear exceptions make delays hard to diagnose.
families.goal: Map the current handoffs, assign decision and data owners, and pilot one reversible improvement with human review intact.
signals: Staff re-enter the same facts across forms, spreadsheets, and a CRM.
A request waits because its next owner or required evidence is unclear.
An automation proposal lacks an exception queue, access boundary, or review checkpoint.
questions: Which handoff loses the most time or context today?
Who can approve a decision, and who resolves an exception?
Which system owns each field, and who may access sensitive records?
paths: Map one real workflow from intake to follow-up and mark wait states.
Separate repeatable status and task updates from decisions reserved for authorized people.
Pilot one reversible handoff with an owner, evidence check, and quality review.
children: Capture complete, consistent intake with clear consent, validation, and a safe path for incomplete submissions.
Organize review inputs and routing logic while keeping eligibility and credit decisions with authorized people.
Track requested records, versions, ownership, and follow-up without exposing documents in ordinary messages.
Route work using documented purpose, product scope, geography, and human review rules.
Make follow-up timing and ownership visible while respecting consent, channel preferences, and opt-outs.
Reduce duplicate entry and missed tasks by defining reliable field ownership, events, and exception handling.
Connect intake, review, documents, decisions, and follow-up through auditable handoffs.

children.headline: Find the funding handoff worth fixing first.
children.summary: Choose where work stalls, how your team operates, and what risk matters most. Get a three-step workflow improvement plan you can review with your team.
children.problemStatement: A funding workflow breaks down at the handoff: missing information, unclear ownership, repeated entry, or follow-up that no one can see.
children.desiredOutcome: Identify one bounded workflow fix, assign its owner and human review point, and protect the source records before automating more.
signals: A request waits without an owner, next action, or due date.
The same applicant facts or document statuses are entered more than once.
A workflow moves forward despite missing evidence or an unresolved exception.
questions: Where does the current request first stall or lose context?
Which update can be automated safely, and which decision requires an authorized reviewer?
What is the source of truth for each field and document status?
paths: Trace one request from intake through follow-up and record each owner, wait state, and system.
Define a narrow rule for the first repeatable handoff, with a visible exception queue.
Review a small pilot against source records before expanding the workflow.
process: Map the current path with the people who perform each step; note missing information and manual re-entry.
Name the system of record, the next owner, and the human approval point for the selected handoff.
Pilot a reversible status or task update; sample results and resolve exceptions before expanding.
considerations: Do not automate eligibility, underwriting, approval, denial, pricing, or lender submission decisions.
Limit access to sensitive information, document consent and retention, and keep source records in their approved system.
Give every exception an owner and a way to stop or reverse the pilot.

FAQs.question: What should be automated first in a funding workflow?
FAQs.answer: Start with the handoff that repeatedly loses status, ownership, or required information. A bounded task or status update is easier to review than an end-to-end decision flow.

FAQs.question: Can this diagnostic decide whether someone qualifies for funding?
FAQs.answer: No. The diagnostic suggests operational improvements from broad workflow choices. Authorized people retain all eligibility, credit, underwriting, approval, pricing, and submission decisions.

FAQs.question: Does the diagnostic store my answers?
FAQs.answer: No. It runs in this browser session, asks for no customer records or credentials, and does not send responses to a server.

children: Evaluate bounded AI assistance for summarization and task support with human review, source traceability, and privacy controls.

families.title: Build business credit with a documented plan
families.summary: Check business records, verify reporting claims, and put payment controls in place. Turn six foundation checks into a practical action roadmap.
families.problem: An account marketed as business credit does not establish that it reports, fits the business, or justifies its cost. Inconsistent identity records and untracked obligations make the next decision harder to support.
families.goal: Know which records are documented, which claims remain unverified, and which actions should come first. Maintain useful foundations without treating a new credit account as a required milestone.
signals: Legal names or identifying information disagree across records you can review.
Reporting claims cannot be matched to current terms or available bureau files.
Payment dates, fees, or the owner of a correction request are unclear.
questions: Which source records substantiate the business identity and any legitimate differences?
What evidence supports each reporting claim, and what remains unconfirmed?
Who reviews payment obligations, cash timing, and changes to account terms?
paths: Use the readiness diagnostic to separate self-reported documentation, needed work, and open verification.
Follow the roadmap to reconcile records, investigate reporting, and organize existing obligations.
If an account serves a business purpose, evaluate written costs, guarantees, and reporting conditions before deciding.

editorial.headline: Build the foundations. Know your next move.
process: Start with the readiness diagnostic: select an objective and review six preparation areas without entering identifying information.
Work through the first three actions using source records, a responsible owner, and a clear completion condition.
Keep the plan current as information, account terms, or operating cash needs change; revisit unresolved reporting claims.
considerations: The diagnostic describes self-reported preparation, not a bureau score, lender requirement, or eligibility decision.
Do not buy accounts solely on a claimed reporting relationship. Confirm current written terms and the evidence relevant to the business.
No universal vendor ladder, number of accounts, or monitoring interval is required by this preparation plan.

FAQs.question: Do I need to open accounts to complete the roadmap?
FAQs.answer: No. The roadmap starts with records and existing obligations. New accounts are optional and should serve an actual business purpose after costs, terms, and payment capacity have been reviewed.

FAQs.question: What does a documented result mean?
FAQs.answer: It means you selected documented answers for the applicable preparation areas. The tool has not accessed records or independently verified your answers, and it does not determine creditworthiness.

FAQs.question: Where should I start if reporting is unclear?
FAQs.answer: Review available business-credit files and ask the provider for current written reporting details, including relevant bureaus and conditions. Keep unavailable or unconfirmed information marked as unresolved.

children: Review foundational business records and reported information to identify items to verify or organize.

children.headline: Check the records behind the business.
children.summary: Compare identity records, business information, and available credit files. Mark discrepancies for verification; this guide does not determine lender eligibility.
children.problemStatement: A legal-name mismatch, outdated contact record, or unexplained reported entry needs a source check. Treating a generic checklist as a lender's approval standard can obscure the actual issue.
children.desiredOutcome: Create a private record-verification log with a source, review date, unresolved issue, and follow-up owner for each item. Keep preparation findings separate from any lender's own requirements.
signals: The business cannot locate current registration or applicable identifier records.
Different records contain information that cannot yet be reconciled or explained.
A report entry disagrees with statements or payment confirmations.
questions: Which current source establishes each identity detail?
Is a difference inaccurate, outdated, legitimate, or still unexplained?
Which source, provider, or bureau owns the information that may need correction?
paths: Build a source checklist for legal name, registration details, applicable identifiers, and contact information; keep values in your own secure records.
Compare available files with account statements and confirmations; record what is visible, unavailable, or unverified.
Use the responsible source's current correction process, retain supporting evidence, and confirm the outcome instead of assuming a request fixed the record.
process: Establish the authoritative source for each item before comparing copies or downstream credit files.
Log the specific mismatch and supporting evidence. Assign the appropriate source or account owner for follow-up.
Review the response and affected record again. Record an unresolved issue as open, with the next verification step.
considerations: Not knowing an answer is a reason to verify, not proof of a negative credit event.
Business-credit files and lender requirements can differ. These preparation steps are not a universal approval checklist.
The linked readiness diagnostic accepts broad selections only. Do not enter identifiers, account details, or personal credit data.

FAQs.question: Is this a lender eligibility or Am I Fundable assessment?
FAQs.answer: No. This page organizes foundational record verification. Its linked business-credit preparation diagnostic identifies tasks from your answers; it does not reproduce a specialized eligibility assessment or make a lender decision.

FAQs.question: What if I cannot access a business-credit file?
FAQs.answer: Keep file visibility marked as unverified and consult the relevant bureau's current official access process. An unavailable file does not by itself establish a negative finding or prove whether an account reports.

FAQs.question: What should a correction log contain?
FAQs.answer: In your own secure records, note the specific entry, source evidence, responsible organization, request date, response, and follow-up step. Recheck the affected record before marking the issue resolved.

children: Sequence identity, record accuracy, monitoring, and responsible account management into a practical plan.

children.headline: A credit roadmap built around evidence.
children.summary: Sequence identity checks, reporting verification, and payment controls into practical work. Use this guide independently or build a plan from the readiness diagnostic.
children.problemStatement: A list of vendors or credit tiers leaves the dependencies unresolved: records may disagree, reporting may be unconfirmed, and existing obligations may already need attention.
children.desiredOutcome: Maintain an evidence-based worklist with a clear source, owner, next action, and completion check. Resolve foundational uncertainty before relying on reporting claims or evaluating an optional account.
signals: Tasks are organized around products instead of the records or controls that need work.
A correction request has been submitted but its outcome has not been checked.
A proposed account has no documented purpose, full cost review, or payment owner.
questions: What must be corrected or verified before the next task can be trusted?
Which existing payment obligation needs immediate ownership?
What evidence will show that an action is complete?
paths: Foundation track: compare current identity and contact records; resolve source discrepancies before relying on downstream files.
Reporting track: review available reports and written reporting conditions, then log unresolved claims and corrections.
Control track: reconcile statements and due dates, review cash capacity and fees, and maintain a documented review process.
process: First, list current source records and explain or correct identity differences. Completion means each material discrepancy has been resolved or clearly marked for follow-up; do not silently assume a match.

Next, review available business-credit files. Compare relevant entries with statements and provider reporting terms. Keep unconfirmed reporting separate from observed entries, and retain correction correspondence.

Address existing obligations as an immediate operating task: assign payment ownership, reconcile confirmations, and investigate unexplained entries. Review cash timing and total costs before any additional commitment.

Maintain the worklist: give each open issue an owner, next action, and completion check. Select report-review timing based on account activity and known issues, and recheck records after correction responses.
considerations: Urgent existing payment problems deserve prompt attention even while identity verification is underway. A numbered sequence is not a reason to delay an obligation.
Before evaluating an account, obtain written fees, payment terms, guarantees, reporting conditions, and cancellation or renewal terms. Compare keeping existing arrangements as a valid option.
There is no required vendor ladder, account purchase, or score target in this roadmap. Bureau processes and lender requirements must be checked with their respective owners.

FAQs.question: Can I use the roadmap without completing the diagnostic?
FAQs.answer: Yes. Use the foundation, reporting, and control tracks above as a worklist. For each task, record the evidence reviewed, unresolved question, owner, next action, and how completion will be confirmed.

FAQs.question: How does the personalized plan change the sequence?
FAQs.answer: The diagnostic prioritizes the gaps you identify, including unknown records and existing payment-control weaknesses. Documented foundations lead to maintenance tasks, while unverified information leads to specific checks rather than assumed failures.

FAQs.question: When is an account-reporting claim verified?
FAQs.answer: Retain current written details about the relevant bureau, what is reported, and any conditions. Compare those claims with available files and provider responses. Do not treat a business-credit label or an absent entry alone as proof.

children: Understand common descriptions of credit-building stages and the limits of vendor-defined tier systems.
Evaluate vendor reporting claims, fees, eligibility, and cancellation terms using current written evidence.
Review payment terms, reporting evidence, minimum purchases, and cash impact before relying on trade credit.
Set a review cadence for business files, identity consistency, inquiries, and disputed information.
Compare fees, guarantees, utilization, and payment controls before adding a revolving account.
Check records, obligations, and payment controls before pursuing additional business credit.

children.headline: Turn what you know into an action plan.
children.summary: Assess six business-credit foundations. See what needs work or verification, then copy a prioritized roadmap with records to review and clear completion checks.
children.problemStatement: An unchecked reporting claim is different from a known record problem, and having no credit accounts is different from mishandling payments. A useful assessment must keep those distinctions visible.
children.desiredOutcome: Leave with a preparation status grounded in your own answers, three immediate actions, remaining verification tasks, and practices for maintaining records and obligations.
signals: Some records are documented while other information is uncertain or inconsistent.
Reporting claims have not been checked against current terms and available files.
Payment tracking, cash reviews, or correction follow-up lacks a practical process.
questions: What evidence supports each documented answer?
Which information needs correction and which simply has not been checked?
Are there existing obligations to reconcile before considering another account?
paths: Choose an objective and answer six questions using documented, needs-attention, or not-sure selections.
Review the evidence register and work through the immediate tasks; each includes what to review and how to recognize completion.
Copy the plan into your own records and use the roadmap and monitoring guides to manage follow-up.
process: Complete the selections without entering names, identifiers, balances, or documents. No existing accounts is an available answer for payment history.
Generate the plan and review its explanation. Documented answers remain self-reported; unknown answers create verification tasks.
Act on the plan, save it if useful, and reassess when the underlying records change. Changing a selection clears the previous result to avoid a stale recommendation.
considerations: This tool never accesses bureau files or independently verifies your answers. Its operational status is not a bureau score, creditworthiness determination, or lender eligibility result.
Answers live only in browser component memory and clear when you leave or reload. Copying exports the readable plan to your device's clipboard.
No purchase, borrowing, vendor enrollment, or new account is required to complete the preparation actions.

FAQs.question: What should I choose when I have not checked a record?
FAQs.answer: Choose not sure / needs verification. The plan will identify evidence to review without inventing a negative finding. Use documented only when you have reviewed supporting records yourself.

FAQs.question: Does the preparation status predict a credit score or approval?
FAQs.answer: No. It describes the completeness of the preparation you reported. The tool does not obtain reports, calculate scores, assess underwriting, or predict a lender's decision.

FAQs.question: How do I save the roadmap?
FAQs.answer: Use Copy Action Plan, or open the readable plain-text plan and copy it manually. The plan includes your objective, preparation findings, tasks, completion criteria, and resource links. No account or email submission is involved.

families.title: Find the cash-flow bottleneck
families.summary: Trace the timing gap between cash in and cash out, then compare operating, customer, inventory, and financing options.
families.problem: A cash shortage can come from timing, margin, growth, seasonality, or obligations. Borrowing may shift timing without fixing the underlying cause.
families.goal: Identify the cause, size, and duration of the gap before choosing an operating or financing response.
signals: Collections regularly arrive after payroll or supplier dates.
Forecasts omit taxes, debt service, or one-time cash needs.
Revenue is rising while available cash is shrinking.
questions: When does the lowest cash point occur, and what drives it?
Which receipts, payments, and assumptions can be verified?
What changes if collections slow or costs rise?
paths: Build a dated cash forecast from actual balances, receivables, payables, and committed costs.
Test collection, purchasing, pricing, and expense changes before adding obligations.
If a structural gap remains, compare suitable funding categories and repayment capacity.
children: Reconcile the cash position, timing, and operating drivers to locate the source of a shortfall.
Project dated inflows and outflows with explicit assumptions, scenarios, and update owners.
Measure the timing and duration between operating cash needs and expected collections.
Plan for payroll timing using confirmed pay dates, collections, tax obligations, and available cash.
Understand how buying, holding, and selling inventory changes cash availability and reorder decisions.
Review invoice aging, disputes, collection ownership, and the cost of delayed customer payment.
Prepare for recurring peaks and troughs with a dated plan for costs, receipts, and reserves.
Test how slower receipts, lower sales, or higher costs affect the lowest projected cash balance.

families.title: Plan the capital move behind growth
families.summary: Connect an expansion goal to its full cost, expected operating impact, timing, and a downside plan.
families.problem: Growth spending can outrun the cash and management capacity needed to deliver the expected return.
families.goal: Build a decision case that accounts for total investment, timing, execution capacity, and slower-than-planned results.
signals: The budget covers purchase price but misses setup or working capital.
Demand assumptions do not have a source or downside case.
Repayment or ongoing costs are not tied to a forecast.
questions: What costs arrive before the investment produces cash?
What evidence supports the demand and margin assumptions?
Can operations deliver the plan if revenue ramps more slowly?
paths: Build a sources-and-uses plan that includes setup, contingency, and operating cash.
Compare a base case with slower sales, higher cost, or delayed opening scenarios.
Select any financing structure only after reviewing repayment, collateral, guarantees, and fit.
children: Estimate the full investment and working-capital needs before committing to a new capacity plan.
Stage site, buildout, staffing, launch, and reserve costs against a realistic opening schedule.
Model recruiting, onboarding, payroll taxes, equipment, and the time before new capacity contributes.
Match purchase quantities and payment timing to sell-through evidence, lead times, and replenishment cash.
Set test budgets and measurable decision gates before committing cash to a campaign or channel.
Compare ownership, lease, and financing costs against equipment use, useful life, and operating cash flow.
Compare total cost, term, collateral, prepayment charges, and cash-flow impact across existing obligations.

families.title: Build a stronger financial operating rhythm
families.summary: Define the planning, reporting, and decision support a business needs before evaluating in-house or outside help.
families.problem: Owners often need forward-looking financial decisions before the business needs or can support a full-time finance executive.
families.goal: Clarify the decisions, reporting cadence, data quality, and accountability required for useful financial leadership.
signals: Reports arrive too late to guide current decisions.
Budgets are not connected to cash forecasts or owners.
Financial analysis depends on one person's undocumented spreadsheet.
questions: Which decisions need a forecast, scenario, or profitability view?
Are accounting records timely and reconciled enough to support analysis?
What scope, cadence, access, and deliverables should an advisor own?
paths: List the recurring business decisions and information each requires.
Improve close, forecast, and reporting ownership before adding advisory scope.
Compare internal, fractional, and external support with explicit responsibilities and controls.
children: Set an operating cadence for cash forecasts, collections, commitments, and variance follow-up.
Translate business priorities into financial assumptions, scenarios, milestones, and review points.
Connect budget owners and actual results to rolling projections and documented assumption changes.
Sequence investment needs, liquidity, debt capacity questions, and decision timing in one plan.
Define a timely, consistent reporting package that supports operating decisions and reconciled records.
Compare contribution and cost-to-serve across products, customers, channels, or locations.
Evaluate growth priorities against cash needs, execution capacity, scenarios, and financing tradeoffs.

families.title: Make financial operations easier to control
families.summary: Improve the workflows, ownership, and data controls behind payments, expenses, revenue, and finance systems.
families.problem: Financial operations become fragile when transactions, approvals, and reconciliations rely on unclear handoffs or disconnected records.
families.goal: Make recurring finance workflows visible, controlled, and easier to reconcile as transaction volume changes.
signals: Approvals happen outside the system of record.
Reconciliations reveal missing context or recurring exceptions.
Several tools hold conflicting versions of key financial data.
questions: Where are ownership, approval, and evidence captured?
Which exceptions recur and what control should prevent them?
How will a change affect reconciliation and audit trails?
paths: Map the transaction from request through approval, posting, and reconciliation.
Clarify policy, system-of-record fields, access, and exception ownership.
Change one workflow at a time and measure error and rework from source records.
children: Map close, payables, receivables, reconciliations, and control ownership across the finance function.
Review payment initiation, approval authority, account controls, settlement visibility, and reconciliation.
Set clear expense policy, documentation, approval, coding, and exception handling.
Align order, billing, collection, and customer records so revenue events reconcile across teams.
Identify repeatable financial tasks and define approvals, audit history, and exception handling before automating.
Assign ownership and quality controls to financial data shared across accounting and operating systems.
Assess bounded AI assistance for finance operations with permission controls, source links, and human review.

families.title: Prepare a clearer funding file
families.summary: Organize business facts, records, obligations, and questions before discussing financing options.
families.problem: Incomplete or inconsistent records make it harder to explain a business's needs and evaluate the obligations of a financing option.
families.goal: Create a documented preparation plan that helps the business and its advisors have a more informed discussion.
signals: Revenue, ownership, or debt figures differ across documents.
The requested amount is not linked to itemized uses and timing.
Repayment capacity has not been considered under a slower-sales scenario.
questions: Can current financial statements be reconciled to source records?
Are planned uses, timing, and existing obligations documented?
Which questions require a lender, attorney, accountant, or other qualified advisor?
paths: Assemble current, internally consistent business and financial records.
Explain the funding purpose, amount, timing, and alternatives considered.
Review costs, covenants, guarantees, and repayment scenarios with qualified professionals.
children: Organize business facts and records into a preparation review; it does not predict approval or eligibility.
List questions a provider may ask and identify which business facts need verification before any application.
Check whether core business and financial records are current, consistent, and easy for an authorized reviewer to follow.
Review credit records, obligations, and identity details and plan how to resolve verified discrepancies.
Reconcile revenue trends, customer concentration, seasonality, and deposits to reliable source records.
Prepare an accurate application checklist with ownership, consent, document dates, and review responsibilities.
Turn identified documentation and planning gaps into a sequenced, owner-assigned preparation plan.

playbookIndex.title: Practical playbooks for the work behind the decision
playbookIndex.summary: Use these operator guides to move from a business problem to an owned workflow, the evidence to gather, a decision check, and a practical next action.

categories.title: Cash Flow
categories.description: Map timing, forecast near-term movement, and test the operating assumptions behind a cash gap.

categories.title: Business Credit
categories.description: Verify business records and account reporting claims before changing or expanding credit activity.

categories.title: Automation
categories.description: Map people, consent, records, handoffs, and exceptions before automating a funding workflow.

categories.title: Growth
categories.description: Test inventory and expansion plans against operating capacity, cash timing, and downside assumptions.

categories.title: Financial Operations
categories.description: Make month-end close, controls, reconciliations, and responsibility clear enough to review.

categories.title: Acquisitions

playbooks.title: Diagnose a Working Capital Gap
playbooks.summary: Trace a cash shortfall to its timing, receivables, inventory, fixed obligations, and revenue variability before choosing a response.
playbooks.audience: Owners and finance operators who see a near-term cash squeeze but need to separate a timing mismatch from a margin, demand, or cost problem.
playbooks.outcome: Leave with a dated cash-gap worksheet, the two or three assumptions that drive the low point, and a named owner for each verification task.
triggers: The bank balance is falling while sales or booked work appear healthy.
Receivables, inventory purchases, payroll, taxes, or debt payments land in different weeks.
A proposed financing or spending decision is being discussed before the size and duration of the gap are known.
evidence: Current bank balances and reconciled cash activity by account.
Open invoices with amount, due date, dispute status, and expected collection evidence.
Inventory on hand, committed purchase orders, lead times, and expected sell-through assumptions.
Fixed obligations with amount, due date, recurrence, and owner.
Recent weekly sales and collections, separated from booked but uncollected revenue.

steps.title: Set the window and starting cash
steps.action: Choose the next 13 weeks or a shorter decision window that covers the expected low point. Reconcile the opening cash figure to bank activity and list restrictions or transfers that make part of the balance unavailable.
steps.completeWhen: The opening amount is tied to a dated bank reconciliation and restricted cash is shown separately.

steps.title: Map expected receipts by evidence
steps.action: List customer receipts by expected week using invoice due dates, payment history, disputes, and customer confirmation. Put uncertain collections in a separate scenario instead of treating a promise or booked sale as cash received.
steps.completeWhen: Every material receipt has a source, expected week, confidence note, and follow-up owner.

steps.title: Map obligations and inventory commitments
steps.action: Schedule payroll, rent, taxes, debt service, supplier invoices, purchase orders, and one-time costs in the week they are expected to clear. Show inventory buys separately from routine purchases so timing and sell-through can be tested.
steps.completeWhen: Known obligations appear once in the correct week and committed inventory cash is visible.

steps.title: Find the lowest point and its drivers
steps.action: Roll opening cash forward as receipts less payments for each week. Identify the first negative or operationally uncomfortable balance, then rank the receipts, costs, and timing assumptions that change it most.
steps.completeWhen: The low point, week, and top drivers are stated without treating the worksheet as an approval or funding result.

steps.title: Test operating responses first
steps.action: Model collection follow-up, purchase timing, inventory quantities, customer deposits, staffing shifts, and discretionary spend as separate changes. Record who must agree and what customer, supplier, legal, or tax terms need confirmation.
steps.completeWhen: Each proposed response has an owner, a measurable assumption, and a review date.

decisionCriteria: A timing gap is plausible when dated receipts lag obligations and the underlying margin and demand assumptions remain supportable.
A recurring deficit or shrinking contribution margin needs an operating and pricing review; moving payment dates alone does not solve it.
Any new financing discussion should use the verified low-point amount, duration, total cost, repayment timing, and downside case.
failureModes: Counting invoices or booked sales as collected cash.
Double-counting a supplier payment and the purchase order that it settles.
Treating all bank cash as available while ignoring restricted funds, payroll, tax, or other commitments.
checklist: Opening cash ties to a recent reconciliation.
Receipt dates are supported and uncertain items are labeled.
Fixed and one-time obligations are assigned to the correct weeks.
Inventory buys and sell-through assumptions are separated.
The low point and its drivers are written down.
Each follow-up has an owner and date.
